scope: Reviewed authored English directions only. No student data.

records.text: One project, four separate stacks. At your already-built walking stick. on start runs once. The two Bluetooth events remember connection changes. forever reads the sensor again and again, chooses one result and sends it. Use your working sensor project. Follow this four-stack plan while keeping the built sensor wiring. Check. near, far and failed-reading unknown belong in different forever branches. The sensor read and message sender repeat together.

Open and protect the working program. In Make Code · Home → your team project. Your working program has the sensor settings that match the built model. A saved copy lets you undo today’s changes. Open the latest team project, then download a backup named WalkingStick_BeforeBluetooth.hex. Check. Your working sensor program is open and backed up. You can see its sensor-reading forever stack. Bluetooth setup alone is not the walking-stick program.

Check the existing sensor once. With your teacher · current sensor program. Keep the sensor blocks, extension and pins that already work. Find the distance in centimetres, written centimetres. Also find how this sensor reports a failed reading. With your teacher, find the forever loop that reads the sensor, the value in centimetres and the test that separates usable readings from failed ones. Check. The teacher has checked all three before you continue. If one is missing, keep the backup and stop here for preparation.

Build the sensor decision inside forever. Inside the existing forever · immediately after the sensor read. The outer if/else checks the reading. Inside its usable path, a second if/else checks the distance. Keep or add an outer Logic if/else after the sensor read, using the checked usable-reading condition. Inside its usable branch, keep or add an if/else comparing your centimetres value ≤ 30. Put X in this inner if, clear screen in its else, and ? in the outer failed-reading branch. Check. If displays are missing, use Basic show icon with X, clear screen, and show string with ?. Add only missing blocks. The next pages add the message assignments.

Add Bluetooth to this project. In Make Code · Extensions. Bluetooth lets the board send messages without a cable. The you art service sends the short text messages that the sound page understands. Open Extensions and add the official Bluetooth extension. Check. Bluetooth blocks appear and the existing sensor blocks remain available.

Use the checked classroom setting. In Make Code · Project Settings. For this supervised demonstration, the teacher checks No Pairing Required. This permits nearby devices to connect. Chrome still asks you to select a device. Select the teacher-approved No Pairing Required setting for this classroom demonstration. Check. The project has the checked setting before it is downloaded.

Fill only the on start stack. Inside on start · not inside forever or an event. on start runs once. Bluetooth uart service prepares the message service. Bluetooth uart write sends a result and belongs later in forever. Create stick status and B T connected in Variables. In on start, keep one set stick status to unknown, one set B T connected to Logic false and one Bluetooth uart service. Remove misplaced near/far setters, extra unknown setters, all you art write blocks, send if blocks and loop pauses from on start. Check. Keep any existing sensor setup. Startup has you art service, not you art write. The result choices and sending blocks will go in forever.

Build the two separate event stacks. Two separate top-level stacks · outside on start and forever. An event runs when something happens. These two events remember when the website connects or disconnects. The sensor loop still controls the display. From Bluetooth, drag on bluetooth connected into an empty workspace area and put set B T connected to true inside it. Beside it, add on bluetooth disconnected with set B T connected to false and set stick status to unknown. Check. Two separate event stacks look like the diagram. Neither event contains sensor reads, near/far decisions or the send block.

Add the near message. forever → usable-reading branch → distance ≤ 30 branch. An if/else chooses one path. The near result belongs inside the usable-reading path, where the checked distance is at or below 30 centimetres. Inside the existing forever stack, find the usable-reading test and its distance ≤ 30 branch. Put set stick status to the text near directly beside the existing X display. Check. near is nested inside both checks. It is not in on start. Exactly 30 centimetres belongs to this near branch.

Add the farther message. forever → usable-reading branch → distance check’s else. This else belongs to the distance check. It runs only when the reading is usable and the distance is above 30 centimetres. Inside the same usable-reading path, find the else paired with distance ≤ 30. Put set stick status to the text far beside the existing clear screen block. Check. far is inside the distance check’s else. Do not put it after near or outside the usable-reading test.

Add the unusable-reading message. forever → failed-reading branch of the outer sensor test. The failed-reading branch is separate from both usable-distance branches. It must not fall through to far. Find the failed-reading branch paired with the outer usable-reading test. Put set stick status to the text unknown beside the existing ? display. Check. Each fresh reading selects only one result: near, far or unknown. unknown does not sit after far in a straight stack.

Send at the bottom of forever. Inside the same forever · after the entire sensor if/else. The complete sensor decision finishes first. The send if is a separate block after that decision, still inside forever. Keep the sensor read. Remove old distance: send blocks and any separate sending loop. After the whole sensor decision, add if B T connected with Bluetooth uart write line stick status inside it. Put one checked pause five hundred after the send if. Check. The send if is not inside near, far, unknown or on start. The pause is inside forever but outside the send if, so it runs even when disconnected.

Compare the complete program. In Make Code · all four stacks before Download. The four stacks work together. The left stacks prepare and remember the connection. The forever stack keeps reading, chooses one result and then sends it. Scroll through all four stacks and compare them with your workspace. Check the two different else branches and the send if after the complete sensor decision. Open the map on its own for a larger view. Check. on start has initial unknown, false and you art service. near/far/failed unknown sit in their own forever branches. The send if and pause are at the bottom of that same forever. The complete map reads as follows. On start: keep any existing sensor setup, set stick Status to unknown, set bee tee Connected to false, and start the Bluetooth you art service. On Bluetooth connected: set bee tee Connected to true. On Bluetooth disconnected: set bee tee Connected to false and stick Status to unknown. In forever: keep the real sensor read in centimetres. If the reading is usable, check whether the distance is at or below thirty centimetres. If it is, show X and choose near. Otherwise, clear the screen and choose far. If the reading was unusable, show a question mark and choose unknown. After this whole decision, if bee tee Connected is true, write the stick Status line over Bluetooth. Outside that sending if, but still inside forever, pause five hundred milliseconds and repeat. Dashed boxes and bracketed labels mean your own existing sensor blocks.

Save and run the updated program. In Make Code · Download, then the MICROBIT drive. A numbered file records the exact program being tested. The simulator cannot prove a physical ultrasonic reading or Bluetooth link. Download the next unused numbered .hex, for example WalkingStick_02.hex. Copy it to the MICROBIT drive using the checked U S B data cable. Check. Wait for copying and flashing to finish. Keep the cable connected until the board is running the updated program.

Open the sound page. In Chrome · a separate tab. The website is already provided. It plays the warning sent by your micro:bit. Browsers wait for a click before allowing sound. Open Walking-stick sounds and click Enable sound. Check. The page is ready to play a warning; connecting is the next step.

Connect your team’s micro:bit. On Walking-stick sounds. Chrome asks which nearby board to connect. Your program must be running on the board you choose. Click Connect micro:bit and select your team’s identified device. Check. The website shows a live connection and receives fresh sensor messages.

Test cardboard at 20 centimetres. At the tabletop model · sound tab visible. This checks the whole path: sensor → program → Bluetooth → website → speaker. Use a ruler, not a guessed distance. Place the cardboard 20 centimetres from the sensor’s front face and observe both displays and the sound. Check. A usable reading near 20 centimetres gives X, near and the near warning.

Move the same cardboard to 40 centimetres. At the tabletop model · sound tab visible. Keep the object and setup the same while changing the distance. The result must come from a valid new reading. Move the cardboard to 40 centimetres from the sensor face and observe again. Check. A usable reading near 40 centimetres gives a blank display and far. The near warning stops.

Check an unusable sensor reading. With your teacher · sound tab visible. The error path matters as much as the near and far paths. Different sensors need different safe invalid-reading tests. Have your teacher run the already-checked unusable-reading test for this model. Check. The board shows ? and the website reports unknown, with the near warning stopped.

Check loss of the connection. On Walking-stick sounds · tabletop model. A disconnected board must not leave an old warning sounding. Separately, more than three seconds without fresh complete messages makes the page show Signal paused. Click Disconnect and check that sound stops. Reconnect the same board and wait for a fresh result. Check. The page shows disconnection, then returns to live sensor messages after reconnecting.

Keep three real trials at each distance. In your existing team test record. One successful try can happen by chance. Repeat the same measured positions so failures are visible too. Run three trials at 20 centimetres and three at 40 centimetres. Record distance, actual reading, board display, website message and sound. Check. Six real trials show what happened, including any failed or missing readings.

Improve one thing and repeat the tests. In the same project and team test record. Changing one thing helps you see what caused a difference. Keep the original observations. Choose one checked correction using the first results. Save the next numbered .hex and copy it to MICROBIT. Wait for transfer to finish, reconnect the sound page, then repeat the same six trials. Check. A separate after-change record can be compared with the original.

Save the final program and results. In your existing team folder and shared report. The saved code should match the program that produced the recorded behavior. The guide itself does not collect answers. Keep the final numbered .hex and actual test notes in the team folder. Update Test and improvement in the shared report. Check. The next editor can find the working version, results and any untested behavior.

Use the existing team handoff. In Google Classroom · existing STEAM assignment. The teacher needs access to the shared report and the final program that your team demonstrates. This is the same project, not another assignment. Have one team member attach the shared report and final numbered .hex to the existing assignment by its announced deadline. Check. The files open for your teacher and match the demonstrated tabletop model.
